payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report

[1] Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot. [2] Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore. [3] This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened. [4] I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.

[5] The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting. [6] Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left. [7] Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon. [8] By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required. [9] Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.

[10] The members learned a great deal from the season. [11] Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day. [12] Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.

[13] Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration. [14] The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it. [15] We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

el_passage.title: The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report
paragraphs: Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot.
Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore.
This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened.
I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.
The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting.
Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left.
Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon.
By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required.
Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.
The members learned a great deal from the season.
Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.
Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration.
The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it.
We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that provides specific evidence for the claim that the members learned a great deal during the season. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Let Cutler's Marsh Flood Again

[1] Behind the Brambleton subdivision, past the last cul-de-sac, lies a flat field of cattails and cracked drainage pipe that most of us have never noticed. [2] Forty years ago it was Cutler's Marsh, until a developer dug ditches to dry it out for houses that were never built. [3] Wetlands are important for many reasons.

[4] This spring the Larkfield town council will vote on whether to spend 180,000 dollars to fill those ditches and let the marsh hold water again. [5] Restoring the marsh would definitely end flooding in Brambleton forever. [6] Last April, after two days of rain, water reached the doorsteps on Finch Lane, and the town paid 64,000 dollars to pump out basements. [7] A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up runoff and releasing it slowly.

[8] Some residents totally freak out about mosquitoes. [9] An ecologist hired by the town, Ilse Varga, reported that a healthy marsh draws dragonflies and frogs that eat mosquito larvae.

[10] Our biology classes could use the marsh as an outdoor lab, measuring water quality instead of just reading about it. [11] Anyway, the council should totally go for it, because it's a no-brainer.

Restoring the marsh would definitely end flooding in Brambleton forever.
Last April, after two days of rain, water reached the doorsteps on Finch Lane, and the town paid 64,000 dollars to pump out basements.
A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up runoff and releasing it slowly.

items.explanation_en:

Speaks directly to student readers through a familiar route and still sets up the field that sentence 2 identifies as the marsh.
"Finch Lane residents still remember the two days of rain last April, when water crept up to their doorsteps and their basements had to be pumped out." is incorrect: Moves the flooding evidence in sentence 6 to the start, so the field that sentence 2 calls Cutler's Marsh is never introduced.
"Honestly, most of us could not care less about some swampy old field behind a subdivision, but maybe we should start caring about it a little." is incorrect: Too casual and dismissive for a paper read by parents and teachers, and it never names the place.
"Since the beginning of human history, people have drained wetlands for farms and towns, and they have often come to regret the choices they made." is incorrect: A sweeping historical claim that loses the local, familiar hook and the specific field.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that addresses parents who may worry about the cost of the project to taxpayers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: At that rate, the 180,000-dollar restoration would cost about as much as three floods like last April's, and the town would not have to pay it again.
options.why: Uses the figures from sentences 4 and 6 to answer a cost worry with a comparison taxpayers can follow.
options.label: correct

options.text: Restoring the marsh would also save the town money on mowing, road salt and school supplies for many decades after the project is done.
options.why: Claims savings that nothing in the draft backs up, and school supplies have nothing to do with the project.
options.label: unsupported

options.text: The water on Finch Lane was muddy and cold, and several families had to move furniture to the upper floors of their homes that weekend.
options.why: Adds vivid detail about the flood but says nothing about cost to taxpayers.
options.label: wrong_scope

options.text: Parents should stop worrying about money, because protecting nature is always worth whatever it ends up costing the town and its taxpayers.
options.why: Brushes off the audience's concern instead of answering it, and the claim is not supported.
options.label: wrong_tone

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that takes a clear position and previews the three benefits discussed in the rest of the editorial. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, mainly because doing so would finally put an end to the flooding on Finch Lane.
options.why: Takes a position but previews only flooding, leaving out mosquitoes and the lab.
options.label: too_narrow

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, because it would ease flooding, keep mosquitoes in check and give our biology classes an outdoor lab.
options.why: Takes an arguable position and previews flooding, mosquitoes and the lab, in the order the paragraphs follow.
options.label: correct

options.text: Although restoring Cutler's Marsh would ease flooding, the costs and the mosquitoes mean the town council should think twice about it.
options.why: Argues against the plan the editorial supports.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Cutler's Marsh was once home to many plants and animals, and people in Larkfield have had different opinions about its future over time.
options.why: States no position and previews none of the editorial's points.
options.label: unsupported

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the sponge comparison connects to the flooding described in sentence 6. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The ditches dug forty years ago, though, are the reason the field is so dry and cracked today, as readers may recall.
options.why: Looks back to sentence 2's history and never ties the sponge to the April flooding.
options.label: illogical_relationship

options.text: Many other towns have restored marshes over the years, and residents there are often quite proud of the work they did.
options.why: Changes the subject to other towns instead of explaining the connection.
options.label: wrong_scope

options.text: Had the marsh been holding water last April, much of that rain would have soaked into it slowly instead of rushing toward Finch Lane.
options.why: Applies the sponge comparison to the April flood, linking the evidence to the claim.
options.label: correct

options.text: Sponges are simple sea animals, and some kinds can soak up many times their own weight in water before they release it.
options.why: Picks up the word sponge but drifts to biology facts with no link to the flood.
options.label: lexical_trap

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 1 and 2 clearly and concisely, keeping both the field's location and the fact that it was once a marsh. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A developer forty years ago drained a field for houses never built that lies behind the Brambleton subdivision and was Cutler's Marsh.
options.why: Keeps the facts, but the modifiers are misplaced, so it sounds as if the houses lie behind the subdivision.
options.label: partially_right

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision there lies, past the very last cul-de-sac, a field that in the past, about forty years ago, was once Cutler's Marsh.
options.why: Wordy and repetitive, and it leaves out the developer's draining.
options.label: wrong_scope

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field of cattails that was, forty years ago, Cutler's Marsh, until a developer drained it for houses never built.
options.why: Keeps the location, the history and the cause in one clear, concise sentence.
options.label: correct

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field, it was Cutler's Marsh forty years ago, until a developer drained it for houses that were never built.
options.why: A comma splice joins two independent clauses.
options.label: convention_error

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field of cattails that was, forty years ago, Cutler's Marsh, until a developer drained it for houses never built.". Keeps the location, the history and the cause in one clear, concise sentence.
"A developer forty years ago drained a field for houses never built that lies behind the Brambleton subdivision and was Cutler's Marsh." is incorrect: Keeps the facts, but the modifiers are misplaced, so it sounds as if the houses lie behind the subdivision.
"Behind the Brambleton subdivision there lies, past the very last cul-de-sac, a field that in the past, about forty years ago, was once Cutler's Marsh." is incorrect: Wordy and repetitive, and it leaves out the developer's draining.
"Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field, it was Cutler's Marsh forty years ago, until a developer drained it for houses that were never built." is incorrect: A comma splice joins two independent clauses.

excluded_items.stem: The writer wants to add a phrase at the beginning of sentence 10 (adjusting capitalization as needed) to show that the outdoor lab is one more benefit added to those already discussed. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

issues.issue: Stray header text 'ALTON original passage' precedes the title and should be removed before delivery.

Title 'Let Cutler's Marsh Flood Again' is intentionally provocative but could momentarily confuse readers, since the argument is that restoration reduces neighborhood flooding. It is acceptable as a rhetorical hook.

Evidence is thin for a draft: the claim that a marsh 'works like a sponge' and the dragonfly and frog point are asserted without much support. This is consistent with a draft that has planned weaknesses, so it is tolerable.
